title: Amazon S3 Revision Notes: Buckets, Storage, Versioning and Access
summary: Quick revision of S3 from the bucket and object model through storage classes, lifecycle rules and versioning to bucket policies, Block Public Access, presigned URLs and consistency. Ends with a night-before cheat sheet.

chapters.title: What This Handbook Covers
points: Buckets and objects
Storage classes
Versioning
Lifecycle rules
Policies, Block Public Access and presigned URLs

chapters.title: Buckets, Objects and Strong Consistency
points: A bucket has a globally unique name and lives in one Region; an object is a key plus data (up to 50 TB) plus metadata, in a flat namespace where 'folders' are only key prefixes containing '/'
A single PUT is capped at 5 GB; use multipart upload above that and preferably above 100 MB, and abort or lifecycle-clean incomplete uploads because they are billed
S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency for PUT, overwrite, DELETE and LIST; there is no eventual-consistency window, and concurrent writers to one key resolve as last writer wins
Everyday usage: aws s3 cp file s3://bucket/key, aws s3 ls s3://bucket/prefix/, aws s3 sync ./dir s3://bucket/dir --delete, aws s3 rm s3://bucket/key --recursive
Interview Point: Is S3 a file system? Is S3 eventually consistent today? What happens when two clients write the same key at once? When do you need multipart upload?

chapters.title: Storage Classes and Lifecycle Rules
points: Classes by access pattern: Standard (frequent), Intelligent-Tiering (unknown or changing, no retrieval fee, auto-tiers), Standard-IA and One Zone-IA (infrequent, millisecond access), Glacier Instant, Glacier Flexible and Deep Archive (archive)

Minimums that bite: Standard-IA and One Zone-IA 30 days and 128 KB billable size, Glacier Instant and Flexible 90 days, Deep Archive 180 days; early delete is still charged; One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ

Retrieval: Glacier Instant is milliseconds; Flexible takes minutes to hours (Expedited, Standard, Bulk); Deep Archive takes hours (Standard about 12h, Bulk about 48h); archived objects need a restore request before GET

Lifecycle rule = filter (prefix, tag, object size) plus Transition action (days after creation, moves only down the class waterfall) plus Expiration action; also set AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload and NoncurrentVersionExpiration; rules run asynchronously about daily

Interview Point: When pick Intelligent-Tiering over IA? Why can lifecycle not move an object back to Standard? Why is transitioning millions of tiny objects to Glacier a cost trap? How do you cut costs of old versions?

chapters.title: Versioning and Delete Behaviour
points: Versioning has three states: unversioned, enabled, suspended; once enabled it can only be suspended, never removed, and existing versions are kept
Each overwrite creates a new version ID; a plain DELETE without a version ID only adds a delete marker, so the object looks gone but older versions remain and are still billed
DELETE with a versionId permanently removes that version; removing the delete marker restores the object; MFA Delete can require MFA for permanent deletes and versioning changes
Enable and inspect: aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket b --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled, then aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket b --prefix key

Interview Point: How do you recover an accidentally deleted object? Why does storage cost grow after enabling versioning and how do you control it? Can you disable versioning? Difference between current and noncurrent version?

chapters.title: Bucket Policies, Block Public Access and Presigned URLs
points: A bucket policy is a resource-based JSON policy (20 KB max) that requires a Principal and can grant cross-account access; an explicit Deny always beats any Allow, and IAM and bucket policy are combined, so same-account access needs an Allow in either
Resource ARNs matter: arn:aws:s3:::bucket applies to bucket actions like ListBucket, arn:aws:s3:::bucket/* applies to object actions like GetObject; using only one is the classic AccessDenied mistake

Block Public Access has four switches (block public ACLs, ignore public ACLs, block public policies, restrict public buckets), works at account and bucket level, overrides policies and ACLs, and is on by default for new buckets; ACLs are disabled by default via Object Ownership BucketOwnerEnforced

Presigned URL: aws s3 presign s3://bucket/key --expires-in 3600 gives time-limited GET access to one object (presigned PUT upload URLs are generated with an SDK, not this command); the default is 3600 s and the max is 7 days with IAM user keys, but it dies earlier with role or session credentials

Interview Point: How do you share a private object temporarily? Why does a presigned URL stop working before expiry? Bucket policy vs IAM policy, which wins? How do you stop public exposure org-wide? Anyone holding a presigned URL can use it, so how do you limit risk?

chapters.title: S3 Cheat Sheet
points: Model: bucket (global unique name, one Region) holds objects (key, up to 50 TB, 5 GB per PUT); flat keys; strong read-after-write consistency; last writer wins
Class minimums: IA 30 days and 128 KB, Glacier Instant and Flexible 90 days, Deep Archive 180 days; Intelligent-Tiering for unknown patterns; archived objects need restore
Versioning: cannot be removed, only suspended; delete adds a marker; versionId delete is permanent; lifecycle expires noncurrent versions and aborts incomplete multipart uploads
Access: explicit Deny wins; bucket ARN versus bucket/* ARN; Block Public Access overrides public policies and ACLs; keep ACLs disabled
Commands: aws s3 cp, sync --delete, ls, rm --recursive, presign --expires-in; aws s3api put-bucket-versioning, put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration, list-object-versions
